title: Policies, processes, procedures, and practices across the organization related to the mapping, measuring, and managing of AI risks are in place, transparent, and implemented effectively.
official: The organization sets up clear, written rules for how AI risks get spotted, measured, and handled, and makes sure everyone actually follows them.
metaphor: Posting the house rules on the fridge (no strangers inside, lock up at night) so everyone knows them and actually follows them, not just a list nobody reads.
translation: Write down simple, plain rules for how your household or small business will handle AI tools, put them somewhere everyone can see, and make sure people really use them.

title: Accountability structures are in place so that the appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks.
official: Specific people are given the authority, the responsibility, and the training to handle AI risks, so it is always clear who owns each job.
metaphor: Deciding who in the family takes out the trash, who walks the dog, and who checks the smoke alarms, so nothing gets forgotten because everyone assumed someone else had it.
translation: Name who is in charge of the AI tools you use, give them the say-so and the know-how to do it, so it is never a mystery who is supposed to handle a problem.

title: Workforce diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility processes are prioritized in the mapping, measuring, and managing of AI risks throughout the lifecycle.
official: A mix of different people and viewpoints is deliberately included when weighing AI risks, so blind spots get caught that one narrow group would miss.
metaphor: Asking everyone at the dinner table, kids and grandparents included, before picking a family vacation, because each person notices problems the others would overlook.
translation: Bring in a range of voices (different ages, backgrounds, and needs) when you judge how an AI tool might help or harm people, since one point of view always misses something.

title: Organizational teams are committed to a culture that considers and communicates AI risk.
official: The whole group builds a habit of thinking about AI risks and talking about them openly, rather than staying quiet when something seems off.
metaphor: A household where anyone can say 'I smell gas' without being brushed off, so worries get spoken out loud instead of bottled up until something goes wrong.
translation: Build a habit where people feel safe raising concerns about AI tools out loud, so problems get talked about early instead of hidden until they blow up.

title: Processes are in place for robust engagement with relevant AI actors.
official: There are real channels for gathering input from the people affected by an AI system, including those who use it and those it makes decisions about.
metaphor: Holding a neighborhood meeting before putting up a big fence, so the people living next door get a genuine say instead of finding out after it is built.
translation: Set up ways to hear from the people your AI tool touches, like customers or staff, and take their feedback in before and after you roll it out.

title: Policies and procedures are in place to address AI risks and benefits arising from third-party software and data and other supply chain issues.
official: The organization has rules for handling the risks that come from AI tools and data built by outside vendors, not just the parts it made itself.
metaphor: Checking that the babysitter and the food delivery service you hire are trustworthy, because a stranger you let into the house is still your responsibility.
translation: Have a plan for the AI tools and data you buy or borrow from other companies, since a weakness in someone else's product can still become your problem.

title: Context is established and understood.
official: Before doing anything else, the team pins down where and why the AI system will be used and who it will affect, setting the stage for every later decision.
metaphor: Before rearranging the furniture, walking through the whole room to see where the doors, outlets, and walkways are, so the plan fits the space you actually have.
translation: Start by understanding exactly what job the AI tool is for, where it will be used, and who it will touch, so every choice after that makes sense for your situation.

title: Categorization of the AI system is performed.
official: The AI system is clearly labeled by what it does and how it works, so its risks can be judged against the right yardstick.
metaphor: Sorting the stuff in your garage into 'tools', 'sharp things', and 'flammable', because you store and handle each pile differently once you know what it is.
translation: Figure out what kind of AI tool you are dealing with and what it actually does, so you can size up its risks against the right expectations.

title: AI capabilities, targeted usage, goals, and expected benefits and costs compared with appropriate benchmarks are understood.
official: The team is honest about what the AI can and cannot do and weighs the expected payoff against the expected cost using sensible comparisons.
metaphor: Reading the real reviews and the price tag before buying a fancy blender, so you know what it can actually do and whether it is worth the money.
translation: Be clear-eyed about what the AI tool can really do, what you hope to gain, and what it will cost you, then check that the benefit is worth the trouble.

title: Risks and benefits are mapped for all components of the AI system including third-party software and data.
official: Every piece of the AI system, including the outside parts, gets its risks and benefits listed out so nothing important is left unexamined.
metaphor: Doing a full walk-around of a used car, tires, brakes, and engine, not just the shiny paint, so you spot the trouble before you buy.
translation: List the good and the risky parts of every piece of your AI tool, including the bits made by other companies, so nothing gets a free pass.

title: Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized.
official: The team thinks through how the AI system could affect real people and the wider world, not just the organization running it.
metaphor: Before starting a loud home renovation, thinking about how the noise and dust will hit not just your family but the neighbors up and down the street.
translation: Think through who could be helped or hurt by your AI tool, from single people to whole communities, so surprises to others do not blindside you later.

title: Appropriate methods and metrics are identified and applied.
official: The team picks the right tests and measurements for the AI system's risks and then actually runs them, instead of guessing.
metaphor: Using a real thermometer and a timer to cook the turkey, rather than poking it and hoping, so you actually know when it is done.
translation: Choose sensible ways to test and measure how your AI tool is doing, then use them, so you are working from facts instead of gut feeling.

title: AI systems are evaluated for trustworthy characteristics.
official: The AI system is checked against the marks of trustworthy AI, such as being safe, fair, private, secure, and understandable.
metaphor: Test-driving a car for brakes, steering, and blind spots before trusting it on the highway, not just admiring how it looks in the driveway.
translation: Actually test whether your AI tool is safe, fair, private, and understandable before you lean on it, instead of assuming it is fine.

title: Mechanisms for tracking identified AI risks over time are in place.
official: There are ongoing ways to keep an eye on known AI risks as time passes, so a small problem does not quietly grow worse.
metaphor: Keeping a chart on the wall for a slow leak under the sink, checking it weekly, so you notice if the drip is getting worse before the floor rots.
translation: Set up a way to keep watching the AI risks you already know about, so you catch a problem that is slowly getting bigger before it becomes a crisis.

title: Feedback about efficacy of measurement is gathered and assessed.
official: The team asks whether their tests and measurements are actually working and adjusts them based on what they learn.
metaphor: Noticing your bathroom scale reads five pounds off, then recalibrating it, because a measuring tool you never double-check can quietly mislead you.
translation: Check that your ways of testing the AI tool are truly telling you the truth, and fix them if they are not, so you are not fooled by bad measurements.

title: AI risks based on assessments and other analytical output from the MAP and MEASURE functions are prioritized, responded to, and managed.
official: Using everything learned so far, the team ranks the AI risks by importance and takes real action on the ones that matter most.
metaphor: After a home inspection lists ten issues, fixing the broken furnace first and the squeaky door last, because you tackle the dangerous stuff before the annoyances.
translation: Take what you learned about your AI tool's risks, put them in order of how serious they are, and deal with the biggest ones first.

title: Strategies to maximize AI benefits and minimize negative impacts are planned, prepared, implemented, documented, and informed by input from relevant AI actors.
official: The team plans and carries out steps to get the most good and the least harm from the AI system, writing it down and shaping it with input from those involved.
metaphor: Planning a road trip to hit the best stops while avoiding the toll roads and traffic, writing the route down, and asking passengers what they want along the way.
translation: Make and follow a written plan to get the most benefit and the least harm from your AI tool, and let the people involved help shape that plan.

title: AI risks and benefits from third-party entities are managed.
official: The risks and rewards coming from outside vendors' AI tools and data are actively handled, not just noticed once and forgotten.
metaphor: Staying on top of the contractor you hired for the roof, checking their work and keeping their number handy, rather than paying up front and hoping for the best.
translation: Keep actively managing the AI tools and data you get from other companies, checking on them over time instead of trusting them once and walking away.

title: Risk treatments, including response and recovery, and communication plans for the identified and measured AI risks are documented and monitored regularly.
official: The steps for responding to and recovering from AI problems, plus who to tell, are written down and checked on a regular basis so they stay ready.
metaphor: Keeping a fire escape plan and a list of emergency numbers on the fridge, then running a drill now and then, so nobody freezes up when something actually happens.
translation: Write down how you will respond to and recover from an AI problem and who you will notify, then review it regularly so the plan is ready when you need it.

title: Prompt Injection
official: Crafted user input or hidden text alters an LLM's behavior or output in ways the designers did not intend, whether the manipulation is directly typed or buried in content the model reads.
metaphor: A stranger tucking a fake note into your kid's lunchbox that tells the babysitter to unlock the front door.
translation: Attackers hide sneaky instructions in the words an AI reads, tricking it into ignoring its rules and doing things you never asked for.

title: Sensitive Information Disclosure
official: An LLM reveals private data, secrets, or proprietary details through its responses, either because that information was in its training or because it was fed in during a conversation.
metaphor: A chatty house guest who repeats your bank PIN and home address to whoever asks over dinner.
translation: The AI can accidentally blurt out private information (passwords, personal records, company secrets) to people who should never see it.

title: Supply Chain
official: Weaknesses enter through the outside pieces an LLM depends on, such as third-party models, training datasets, and software libraries, any of which can be tampered with or poorly vetted.
metaphor: Building your house with lumber and locks from a stranger's truck, never checking whether any of it is rotten or rigged.
translation: AI systems are assembled from borrowed models, data, and code; if any of those outside parts is tampered with or flawed, the whole system inherits the problem.

title: Data and Model Poisoning
official: Attackers corrupt the data used to train or fine-tune a model, planting biases, backdoors, or flaws that quietly shape how the model behaves later.
metaphor: Someone slipping bad ingredients into the flour bin so every loaf your family bakes for months comes out tainted.
translation: If the examples an AI learns from are secretly rigged, the finished model carries hidden flaws or backdoors that show up long after training.

title: Improper Output Handling
official: An application trusts and forwards an LLM's output without validating or cleaning it first, letting whatever the model produced flow straight into other systems and cause harm.
metaphor: Letting your kid read a mystery text message aloud and acting on it instantly, without ever checking who really sent it.
translation: When software blindly trusts whatever the AI spits out and passes it along unchecked, malicious content can slip through and damage other systems.

title: Excessive Agency
official: An LLM is handed too much power, too many tools, or too broad a set of permissions, so a bad decision or a hijacked prompt can trigger real-world actions well beyond what was needed.
metaphor: Giving the house-sitter the keys to your car, your safe, and your bank account when all they needed was to feed the cat.
translation: When an AI is allowed to take actions and touch systems far beyond its job, a single mistake or manipulation can cause outsized real-world damage.

title: System Prompt Leakage
official: The hidden setup instructions that govern an LLM get exposed, revealing rules, secrets, or logic that were meant to stay behind the scenes and can then be exploited.
metaphor: Leaving the babysitter's private instruction sheet, including the alarm code, taped to the front window for anyone to read.
translation: The behind-the-scenes rules that guide an AI can leak out, and once attackers see those instructions they can find the gaps and work around them.

title: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
official: Flaws in how a system generates, stores, or retrieves the numeric representations behind retrieval-augmented generation let attackers poison the knowledge store or pull out information they should not access.
metaphor: A home filing cabinet with a broken lock, where anyone can slip in fake documents or read the family's private folders.
translation: AI systems that look up stored knowledge can be attacked through that memory bank, letting bad actors plant false facts or steal what is filed there.

title: Misinformation
official: An LLM produces false or fabricated statements that sound convincing, and people relying on the system act on that wrong information as if it were true.
metaphor: A know-it-all neighbor who confidently gives you wrong directions, so you drive an hour the wrong way trusting them.
translation: AI can state made-up or incorrect facts in a confident tone, and if you trust it without checking, you end up acting on things that simply are not true.

title: Unbounded Consumption
official: An LLM is allowed to run without sensible limits, so attackers can flood it with heavy requests that drain computing resources, run up costs, or knock the service offline.
metaphor: A guest who leaves every faucet and the garden hose running all day, spiking your water bill until the tank runs dry.
translation: Without caps on how much work an AI will do, attackers can overload it with expensive requests, racking up huge bills or crashing the service for everyone.

title: Reconnaissance
official: The adversary gathers information about a target's AI systems to plan later operations, using techniques such as Search Open Technical Databases, Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis, and Active Scanning.
metaphor: Casing a house from the sidewalk before a break-in: noting which doors have locks, where the cameras point, and when the family leaves for work.
translation: Before attacking an AI system, adversaries study it: what model it runs, how it was built, any publicly reported weaknesses, and where its soft spots are.

title: Resource Development
official: The adversary builds, buys, or steals the resources needed to support an attack, using techniques such as Acquire Public AI Artifacts, Develop Capabilities, and Publish Poisoned Datasets.
metaphor: A burglar assembling a kit before the job: buying lock picks, copying a key, and parking a getaway van a block away.
translation: Attackers set up their toolkit: grabbing public models and datasets, writing malware, renting servers and accounts, or seeding tampered data for later use.

title: Initial Access
official: The adversary tries to gain a first foothold in the AI system, using techniques such as AI Supply Chain Compromise, Valid Accounts, and Exploit Public-Facing Application.
metaphor: Getting through the front door the first time: a stolen key, an unlocked window, or a tampered package left on the porch.
translation: Attackers find a way in: poisoning the AI supply chain, stealing valid logins, phishing staff, or exploiting an internet-facing application.

title: AI Model Access
official: The adversary seeks some level of access to the AI model itself, using techniques such as AI Model Inference API Access, AI-Enabled Product or Service, and Full AI Model Access.
metaphor: Getting close to the safe: peering through the keyhole, using it as a paying customer, or holding the full combination and its internal workings.
translation: Attackers get their hands on the model, from simply querying its API to fully accessing its internals, so they can probe it, feed it data, and craft attacks.

title: Execution
official: The adversary tries to run malicious code or instructions on the system, using techniques such as LLM Prompt Injection, User Execution, and AI Agent Tool Invocation.
metaphor: Tricking someone inside the house into carrying out your orders, like slipping a fake instruction into the family's chore list.
translation: Attackers get the AI system to run their code or hidden instructions, for example by smuggling commands into a prompt that an LLM or agent then obeys.

title: Persistence
official: The adversary tries to keep their foothold across restarts and cleanups, using techniques such as Poison Training Data, Manipulate AI Model, and RAG Poisoning.
metaphor: Hiding a spare key under the mat so you can slip back in even after the family changes the locks.
translation: Attackers plant lasting backdoors in the AI: poisoned training data, a tampered model, or corrupted knowledge sources, so they keep access after reboots and fixes.

title: Privilege Escalation
official: The adversary tries to gain higher-level permissions, using techniques such as LLM Jailbreak, AI Agent Tool Invocation, and Escape to Host.
metaphor: A guest let into the living room finding the master key and quietly unlocking every other room in the house.
translation: Attackers turn limited access into broad control: jailbreaking an LLM past its guardrails, abusing an agent's tools, or breaking out onto the host machine.

title: Defense Evasion
official: The adversary tries to avoid detection by AI-enabled defenses, using techniques such as Evade AI Model, LLM Prompt Obfuscation, and LLM Jailbreak.
metaphor: Wearing a disguise and stepping around the security cameras so the guard dog never barks.
translation: Attackers dodge AI-based detection: crafting inputs that slip past malware or content filters, or disguising prompts so the model never flags them.

title: Credential Access
official: The adversary tries to steal account names and passwords, using techniques such as Unsecured Credentials, RAG Credential Harvesting, and Credentials from AI Agent Configuration.
metaphor: Rifling through the kitchen drawers for the sticky note where someone wrote down all the passwords.
translation: Attackers hunt for logins and keys, pulling secrets out of AI agent configs, knowledge bases, or carelessly stored credentials to unlock more of the system.

title: Discovery
official: The adversary tries to map the AI environment from the inside, using techniques such as Discover AI Model Family, Discover AI Artifacts, and Discover LLM System Information.
metaphor: Once inside, wandering room to room to learn the layout: where the valuables sit and which doors lead where.
translation: Now inside, attackers explore the AI setup: which model family it is, what data and artifacts exist, and how it is configured, to plan their next move.

title: Lateral Movement
official: The adversary tries to move through the AI environment to reach other systems, using techniques such as Use Alternate Authentication Material and Phishing.
metaphor: Having slipped into one room, using a found keycard to move down the hall into the offices and storage closets.
translation: Attackers pivot from their entry point to other systems, like model registries, notebooks, or training pipelines, often reusing stolen keys or hijacking over-privileged AI agents.

title: Collection
official: The adversary gathers the AI artifacts and data relevant to their goal, using techniques such as AI Artifact Collection, Data from Information Repositories, and Data from AI Services.
metaphor: Going through the house and piling everything worth taking, jewelry, documents, electronics, by the back door.
translation: Attackers scoop up the valuable material: models, training data, and files from repositories, local systems, and AI services, staging it to steal or reuse.

title: AI Attack Staging
official: The adversary prepares and tunes the attack on the target model, using techniques such as Create Proxy AI Model, Craft Adversarial Data, and Verify Attack.
metaphor: Buying the exact same lock as your target and practicing on it at home until you can pick it in seconds.
translation: Attackers rehearse offline: building a copycat model, crafting tricky inputs, or tampering with the model, then verifying the attack works before firing it for real.

title: Command and Control
official: The adversary tries to communicate with and remotely control compromised AI systems, using techniques such as Reverse Shell, AI Service API, and AI Agent.
metaphor: A burglar leaving a walkie-talkie hidden inside so an accomplice outside can quietly relay orders.
translation: Attackers set up a hidden channel to steer a compromised AI system from afar, often disguising the traffic as ordinary API calls or normal agent activity.

title: Exfiltration
official: The adversary tries to steal AI artifacts and other data, using techniques such as Exfiltration via AI Inference API, Extract LLM System Prompt, and LLM Data Leakage.
metaphor: Carrying the loot out of the house, whether stuffed in a backpack or smuggled out little by little with the trash.
translation: Attackers spirit data out: model weights, training data, or secrets, by coaxing an LLM to leak its prompt or answers, or by channeling data through the inference API.

title: Impact
official: The adversary tries to manipulate, disrupt, erode confidence in, or destroy AI systems and data, using techniques such as Denial of AI Service, Erode AI Model Integrity, and Cost Harvesting.
metaphor: Trashing the house on the way out: smashing things, jamming the locks, and running up the utility bills out of spite.
translation: Attackers cause the real damage: knocking the AI offline, degrading its accuracy, running up huge compute bills, or using its outputs to harm people and erode trust.

title: Search Open Technical Databases
official: Adversaries search publicly available research and technical documentation to learn how and where AI is used inside a victim organization, then use that knowledge to pick targets or tailor an attack. Academic papers, preprint servers, and conference talks by the victim's own staff are common sources.
metaphor: Reading a company's published architectural plans at the library before deciding which wall to knock through.
translation: Teams publish more about their AI than they realize. Papers, patents, and conference talks name the model architecture, the training approach, and often the people who built it, which is exactly the head start an attacker wants.

title: Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis
official: Adversaries look for pre-existing published research on weaknesses in the class of model a target uses, including known attack methods, published adversarial examples, and reproduction code. Reusing someone else's analysis is cheaper than developing an attack from scratch.
metaphor: Checking whether a lock model already has a known bypass posted online before trying to pick it yourself.
translation: Most AI attacks do not need to be invented. If the target runs a well-known model family, the weaknesses are usually documented in public research, often with working code attached.

title: Search Victim-Owned Websites
official: Adversaries mine the victim's own websites for information useful during targeting: product pages describing AI features, engineering blogs, documentation, careers listings, and staff directories that reveal who works on what.
metaphor: Learning the layout of a shop from its own website before walking in, including which staff work the back office.
translation: Your marketing site, docs, and job postings describe your AI stack in more detail than you would ever give a stranger who asked. Attackers read all of it first.

title: Search Application Repositories
official: Adversaries browse open application repositories such as Google Play, the iOS App Store, the macOS App Store, and the Microsoft Store to find applications that use AI, then download and inspect them for embedded models and endpoints.
metaphor: Buying a competitor's appliance off the shelf so you can take it apart on your own workbench.
translation: Shipping a model inside a mobile app hands a copy to anyone who downloads it. App stores are a browsable catalog of AI systems an attacker can study offline at leisure.

title: Active Scanning
official: An adversary probes the victim system directly to gather targeting information, in contrast to reconnaissance methods that only read public sources. Scanning can reveal exposed inference endpoints, supported input formats, rate limits, and error behavior.
metaphor: Walking the perimeter and trying every door handle rather than reading the floor plan from home.
translation: Rather than researching from a distance, the attacker pokes the system and watches how it answers. Error messages, timing, and rate-limit responses all leak details about what is behind the endpoint.

title: Gather RAG-Indexed Targets
official: Adversaries identify the data sources a retrieval augmented generation system indexes, so that later poisoning or manipulation can be aimed at repositories the model will actually read. Public wikis, ticket systems, shared drives, and crawled sites are common targets.
metaphor: Finding out which newspaper the household reads before planting a story in it.
translation: A RAG system is only as trustworthy as the documents it retrieves. Attackers first work out which sources get indexed, because that is where a planted document will be picked up and repeated as fact.

title: Gather Victim Identity Information
official: Adversaries collect identity details about the victim organization and its people, including employee names, roles, email addresses, and credentials exposed in breaches, for use in later targeting.
metaphor: Copying names off the staff photo board in a lobby so a later phone call sounds like it comes from a colleague.
translation: Knowing who works on the AI platform, what they are called, and how their email addresses are formed is what makes a later phishing message or account takeover attempt believable.

title: Search Open Websites/Domains
official: Adversaries search public websites and domains for information about a victim, including social media, search engines, code-hosting sites, and paste sites. These sources can expose infrastructure details, staff activity, and leaked artifacts.
metaphor: Piecing together a family's routine from what they post publicly, without ever going near the house.
translation: Search engines, social posts, and public repositories add up. Individually harmless details combine into a picture of who runs the AI system, what it is built on, and when nobody is watching it.

title: Acquire Public AI Artifacts
official: Adversaries collect AI artifacts from public sources such as cloud storage, public-facing services, and software or data repositories. Datasets, model weights, and configuration files obtained this way support later attack staging.
metaphor: Taking the free sample home so you can analyze the recipe at your own kitchen table.
translation: Published models and datasets are convenient for developers and equally convenient for attackers, who use the same downloads to build an offline copy of what you run in production.

title: Acquire Infrastructure
official: Adversaries buy, lease, or rent infrastructure to support their operation, including servers, domains, cloud accounts, and the GPU capacity needed to train or run models. Rented infrastructure is disposable and hard to attribute.
metaphor: Renting an anonymous storage unit across town to work out of instead of using your own garage.
translation: Attacks on AI need compute. Renting cloud GPUs and throwaway domains gives an adversary the horsepower to train proxy models and somewhere to point traffic that leads nowhere back to them.

title: Obtain Capabilities
official: Adversaries acquire existing software capabilities for use in their operations, including adversarial machine learning toolkits, exploit code, and commercial or open source offensive tools, rather than building their own.
metaphor: Buying professional tools at the hardware store rather than forging them yourself.
translation: Mature tooling for attacking models already exists and much of it is open source and well documented. Buying or downloading is faster than building, so most adversaries do exactly that.

title: Develop Capabilities
official: Adversaries build their own capabilities to support operations when nothing suitable exists off the shelf, including custom adversarial example generators, poisoning pipelines, and purpose-built malware.
metaphor: Machining a custom key when no blank on the rack fits the lock.
translation: When a target is unusual enough that public tools do not work, a determined adversary writes their own. Custom tooling is slower to build and much harder for defenders to recognize.

title: Training Data Poisoning
official: Adversaries manipulate the data used to train or fine-tune a model so that the resulting model behaves the way they want. Poisoning can degrade accuracy broadly or install a targeted backdoor that only activates on a chosen trigger.
metaphor: Slipping a few wrong entries into an apprentice's textbook so they confidently learn one thing incorrectly.
translation: A model is the sum of what it was shown. Corrupt a small slice of the training set and you can make the model fail on demand, often without anyone noticing that overall accuracy barely moved.

title: Establish Accounts
official: Adversaries create accounts with services for use in targeting, to obtain the access needed for attack staging, or to impersonate a victim. Accounts on model hubs, cloud platforms, and social services all serve this purpose.
metaphor: Opening a bank account under a business name you invented, purely so the paperwork looks legitimate later.
translation: A brand new account on a model hub or cloud platform costs nothing and gives an attacker a legitimate-looking identity to publish from, request quota with, or impersonate someone under.

title: Publish Hallucinated Entities
official: Adversaries register an entity that a language model invents, such as a package name, website, or email address the model recommends but that does not exist, then fill it with adversary-controlled content so the model's advice leads users to them.
metaphor: A confident tour guide keeps sending visitors to a restaurant that was never there, so you open one at that address and wait.
translation: Language models invent plausible package names and URLs. If a model reliably hallucinates the same one, an attacker registers it, and every developer who follows the model's advice installs their code.

title: LLM Prompt Crafting
official: Adversaries use what they have learned about a target generative AI system to write prompts that get past its defenses and cause malicious instructions to run. Crafting is usually iterative, refined against observed refusals.
metaphor: Rehearsing exactly how to word a request to a strict receptionist until one phrasing gets you waved through.
translation: Prompt attacks are rarely one lucky sentence. The adversary probes what gets refused, learns the shape of the guardrail, and rewrites until a phrasing slips past it.

title: Retrieval Content Crafting
official: Adversaries author content designed to be retrieved by user queries and to influence the user or the system when it is surfaced. The content is written to rank well for target queries and to carry instructions or misinformation.
metaphor: Writing a pamphlet specifically so it ends up in the doctor's waiting room, aimed at whoever picks it up.
translation: If you know what a retrieval system searches for, you can write a document engineered to be the one it finds. Whatever that document says then arrives with the system's authority behind it.

title: Stage Capabilities
official: Adversaries upload, install, or otherwise position capabilities where they can be used during targeting, such as placing a poisoned model on a hub, hosting a malicious payload, or seeding a repository ahead of time.
metaphor: Hiding the ladder in the hedge days before the night you plan to use it.
translation: Attack tooling gets put in place before the attack. A poisoned model uploaded to a hub or a payload parked on a rented domain sits quietly until the moment it is needed.

title: Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts
official: Adversaries create or modify AI artifacts and publish them through public or shared distribution channels so downstream systems are compromised when they consume them. Poisoned datasets, models, and agent tools may carry malicious content, behaviors, code, or configuration, published as novel artifacts or as malicious variants of legitimate ones.
metaphor: Printing a counterfeit edition of a trusted cookbook, one ingredient changed, and getting it onto the shop shelf beside the real one.
translation: Model hubs, dataset repositories, package registries, and tool directories are supply chains. An artifact published there with a familiar-looking name can be pulled into a hundred systems that never inspected it.

title: AI Supply Chain Compromise
official: Adversaries gain initial access by compromising the parts of the supply chain specific to AI: the data, the model, the ML software stack, or the hardware. A compromise upstream reaches every system that consumes the artifact.
metaphor: Contaminating something at the bottling plant rather than breaking into each house that buys a bottle.
translation: AI systems are assembled from other people's datasets, weights, and libraries. Compromising one widely used component gets the attacker into every product built on top of it.

title: Valid Accounts
official: Adversaries obtain and abuse the credentials of existing accounts to gain initial access. Legitimate credentials blend into normal activity and often bypass controls aimed at detecting intrusion.
metaphor: Walking in the front door with a key that works, so nobody thinks to question you.
translation: The quietest way into an AI platform is a real login. Stolen or leaked credentials produce activity that looks authorized, because as far as the system is concerned it is.

title: Evade AI Model
official: Adversaries craft adversarial data or generate deepfakes so that a model misclassifies input or accepts fabricated content as authentic. Evasion can be used to slip past AI-based detection or to gain access to a system that gates on model output.
metaphor: Wearing a disguise that the face-recognition doorman waves through without a second look.
translation: When a model is the gate, fooling the model is the way in. Small, deliberate changes to an input can flip its verdict while a person looking at the same input notices nothing odd.

title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
official: Adversaries exploit a weakness in an internet-facing computer or program using software, data, or commands to cause unintended behavior. In AI systems this often means the serving layer, the notebook environment, or the orchestration around the model rather than the model itself.
metaphor: Prying open a badly fitted window on the ground floor instead of arguing with the doorman.
translation: The model is often the best-defended part of the stack. The inference server, the notebook host, and the API gateway around it are ordinary software with ordinary vulnerabilities.

title: Phishing
official: Adversaries send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. Messages may carry malicious attachments or links, and in AI contexts may target the engineers and data scientists who hold access to models and pipelines.
metaphor: A letter on convincing headquarters letterhead asking a branch manager to confirm the safe combination.
translation: The people who can reach your training pipeline get email like everyone else. Phishing remains the most reliable way in, and AI teams are a high-value inbox to target.

title: Drive-by Compromise
official: Adversaries gain access through a user visiting a website in the ordinary course of browsing, or through an AI agent retrieving web content on a user's behalf. The malicious content executes without any deliberate download.
metaphor: Picking up something contagious just by sitting in the waiting room, having touched nothing.
translation: Ordinary browsing is enough. When an AI agent fetches pages for a user, the agent becomes the one visiting hostile sites, and it does so far more often than any person would.

title: Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application
official: An adversary plants malicious prompts in a victim's public-facing application so that an AI system ingests them later and acts on them. Support tickets, reviews, form submissions, and user profiles are all channels into a system's future context.
metaphor: Writing instructions in the suggestion box, knowing management reads it aloud at the Monday meeting.
translation: Anything a customer can type may end up inside a model's context window later. A support ticket written as an instruction becomes an instruction the moment an AI assistant reads the queue.

title: AI Model Inference API Access
official: Adversaries obtain access to a model through its legitimate inference API. Query access alone is enough to support extraction, evasion development, and probing for training data.
metaphor: Learning how a vending machine works by feeding it coins all day, never once opening the cabinet.
translation: You do not need the weights to attack a model. Enough queries against a public API reveal its decision boundaries, and sometimes enough to rebuild a usable copy of it.

title: Physical Environment Access
official: Adversaries exploit the physical environment a model perceives rather than the digital system, for example by altering objects, lighting, or signage that a sensor-driven model interprets.
metaphor: Putting a sticker on a road sign so the driver reads it wrong, without touching the car at all.
translation: Models that see the world can be attacked through the world. A sticker, a printed pattern, or a change in lighting can fool a vision system while the network and servers stay untouched.

title: Full AI Model Access
official: Adversaries gain full white-box access to a model, including its architecture, parameters, and gradients. This is the strongest position for developing evasion and extracting information about training data.
metaphor: Having the safe's blueprints, not just the chance to spin the dial and listen.
translation: With the weights in hand an attacker can compute exactly which changes to an input will flip the model's answer, instead of guessing. Everything downstream gets easier and more reliable.

title: AI-Enabled Product or Service
official: Adversaries use a product or service that runs AI under the hood in order to reach the underlying model indirectly, obtaining query access through the ordinary user interface.
metaphor: Studying the chef's technique by ordering from the menu every night, since the kitchen is closed to visitors.
translation: Any shipped feature that calls a model is a way to query that model. The consumer interface is often less monitored and less rate-limited than the API it sits on top of.

title: User Execution
official: An adversary relies on a person to load, execute, interpret, or otherwise use a malicious or unsafe artifact. Notebooks, model files, and pickled objects all run code when opened, so the user does the work of executing the payload.
metaphor: Handing someone a package and letting them open it for you, because the box only opens from the inside.
translation: Many AI file formats execute code when they load. An attacker does not need to break in if a data scientist will download the model and open the notebook for them.

title: Command and Scripting Interpreter
official: Adversaries abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. In AI environments this commonly means shells reachable from a notebook, a training job, or a tool an agent is allowed to call.
metaphor: Once inside the building, using the intercom system that was already wired to every room.
translation: Interpreters are already there and already trusted. A notebook cell, a training entrypoint, or an agent's shell tool gives an attacker ordinary command execution inside your AI environment.

title: LLM Prompt Injection
official: An adversary crafts malicious prompts as input to a language model so that it acts in unintended ways. Injection may be direct, typed by the adversary, or indirect, planted in content the model later reads.
metaphor: Slipping a forged note into the stack a messenger is carrying, so the next instruction they follow is yours.
translation: Language models do not reliably separate instructions from data. Text that arrives inside a document, a web page, or an email can be read as a command and obeyed.

title: AI Agent Tool Invocation
official: Adversaries use their access to an AI agent to invoke the tools that agent is permitted to call. The agent's own permissions become the adversary's, without any credential of their own.
metaphor: Persuading someone with a master key to open the door for you, so your name never appears on the access log.
translation: An agent's tools are its hands. Whoever can steer the agent can reach every system, file, and API the agent was trusted with, using the agent's credentials rather than their own.

title: AI Agent Clickbait
official: Adversaries craft deceptive web content designed to bait computer-using agents or AI browsers into unintended actions such as clicking buttons, copying code, or navigating to adversary-controlled pages.
metaphor: Painting a fake door on a wall, convincing enough that an eager assistant walks straight into it.
translation: Agents that browse the web click things. Content built to look like the next obvious step to a machine, rather than to a person, can steer an agent somewhere it should never have gone.

title: Deploy AI Agent
official: Adversaries launch AI agents inside the victim environment to carry out actions on their behalf, using the environment's own compute, credentials, and network position.
metaphor: Hiring a temp who reports to you, sitting them at a desk inside the office, and letting them do the rounds.
translation: Instead of running the attack themselves, the adversary starts an agent in your environment and lets it work. It looks like internal automation and it operates at machine speed.

title: Manipulate AI Model
official: Adversaries alter a model artifact or its bundled components to change system behavior, introduce malicious code, or install persistent malicious functionality. The change may target weights, architecture, or the serialization format itself.
metaphor: Rewiring an appliance so it works normally until the one day you flip a hidden switch.
translation: A model file is code and data together. Editing it can install behavior that survives restarts and redeployments, because the backdoor ships inside the artifact everyone trusts.

title: LLM Prompt Self-Replication
official: An adversary crafts a prompt injection designed to make the model reproduce the injected prompt in its own output, so the instruction spreads into subsequent contexts, documents, and conversations.
metaphor: A chain letter that instructs each reader to copy it out again before passing it on.
translation: An injected instruction that tells the model to repeat itself will end up in summaries, replies, and saved notes. From there it gets read by the next model and the infection keeps going.

title: RAG Poisoning
official: Adversaries inject malicious content into the data a retrieval augmented generation system indexes, contaminating future threads through the search results the system returns.
metaphor: Filing a forged document in the reference cabinet, so every clerk who looks it up cites it as fact.
translation: Poison the corpus and you poison every answer drawn from it. The model behaves correctly; it is faithfully repeating a document that should never have been in the index.

title: AI Agent Context Poisoning
official: Adversaries manipulate the context an agent's language model works from, influencing the responses it generates and the actions it takes. Memory files, scratchpads, prior turns, and retrieved documents are all context.
metaphor: Editing the notes someone left themselves overnight, so the plan they wake up and follow is not the one they wrote.
translation: An agent's context is its working memory. Anything an attacker can write into that memory shapes every decision the agent makes afterward, long after the original injection.

title: Modify AI Agent Configuration
official: Adversaries modify the configuration files that govern AI agents on a system, changing tool permissions, system prompts, model endpoints, or safety settings.
metaphor: Quietly rewriting the standing orders pinned above the night guard's desk.
translation: Agent behavior lives in config: which tools it may call, what its system prompt says, which endpoint it talks to. Edit that file and you have changed the agent permanently without touching its code.

title: AI Agent Tool Data Poisoning
official: Adversaries manipulate data in a victim-controlled, trusted, or connected source that an agent reaches through one of its tools, so the agent acts on falsified information.
metaphor: Changing the numbers in the ledger the accountant checks, rather than arguing with the accountant.
translation: Agents trust what their tools return. Corrupting the database, ticket queue, or file share behind a tool means the agent reasons correctly from data that is a lie.

title: AI Agent Tool Poisoning
official: Adversaries poison the tools an agent uses by introducing or modifying malicious content or behavior in a tool's model-visible definition, its executable implementation, or its runtime responses.
metaphor: Relabeling the jars in a kitchen so the recipe is followed exactly and the dish still comes out wrong.
translation: A tool's description is text the model reads and believes. Malicious wording in a tool definition, or a tool that returns instructions instead of data, redirects the agent while every step looks legitimate.

title: LLM Jailbreak
official: Adversaries induce a language model to ignore, circumvent, or override its safety and alignment behavior in order to elicit output the model was intended to withhold. Techniques include role play, encoding, and multi-turn pressure.
metaphor: Talking a rule-following clerk into an exception, one small concession at a time, until the rule no longer applies.
translation: Guardrails are behavior, not walls. Enough framing, indirection, and persistence will usually convince a model that this particular request is the exception.

title: Escape to Host
official: Adversaries break out of a container or virtualized environment to reach the underlying host, expanding access from a single workload to the machine running it and everything else on it.
metaphor: Getting out of the hotel room and into the service corridor that opens onto every other room.
translation: Training and inference workloads run in containers. An escape turns a compromised job into control of the host, its GPUs, and any other tenant sharing it.

title: LLM Trusted Output Components Manipulation
official: Adversaries use prompts that manipulate components of a model's response, such as citations, source links, or formatting, to make the answer appear more trustworthy than it is.
metaphor: Attaching an official-looking seal and reference number to a letter you wrote yourself.
translation: People judge an answer by its trappings. Fabricated citations, invented source links, and confident formatting make a poisoned response read like a well-researched one.

title: LLM Prompt Obfuscation
official: Adversaries hide or obfuscate prompt injections and retrieval content to avoid detection by humans, model guardrails, or other detection mechanisms. Encoding, invisible characters, and unusual formatting are common.
metaphor: Writing the instruction in lemon juice, invisible until the right lamp is held over it.
translation: An injection does not have to be readable to work. White text, zero-width characters, base64, and image-embedded text all reach the model while a reviewer sees nothing.

title: False RAG Entry Injection
official: Adversaries insert fabricated entries into a victim's retrieval augmented generation database so the system retrieves and repeats content that was never legitimate.
metaphor: Adding an invented entry to the encyclopedia, complete with the right typeface, so nobody questions it.
translation: A retrieval database is usually trusted without further checking. A single planted record will be surfaced, cited, and repeated as though it came from the organization itself.

title: Impersonation
official: Adversaries impersonate a trusted person or organization to persuade a target into acting on their behalf. Generative models make convincing voice, video, and written impersonation cheap.
metaphor: Turning up in the uniform of the utility company, clipboard in hand, and being shown to the basement.
translation: Trust is a shortcut people take. Synthesized voice and text now make a convincing impersonation quick to produce, so the usual cues of authenticity no longer prove much.

title: Masquerading
official: Adversaries manipulate features of their artifacts so those artifacts appear legitimate or benign to users and security tools, including names, metadata, file properties, and repository presentation.
metaphor: Putting the real brand's label on a counterfeit tin so it passes on the shelf.
translation: A malicious model or package that carries a familiar name, a plausible author, and tidy documentation gets installed. Most reviews check the label rather than the contents.

title: Corrupt AI Model
official: An adversary deliberately corrupts a malicious model file so it cannot be fully deserialized, causing a model scanner to fail or skip the file while the target's loader still reaches the payload.
metaphor: Damaging a parcel just enough that the scanner rejects it and a human waves it through by hand.
translation: Scanners have to parse a file to inspect it. Breaking the format in a way that defeats the scanner but not the loader is a way to be neither read nor blocked.

title: Manipulate User LLM Chat History
official: Adversaries alter a user's chat history with a language model to conceal malicious activity, removing or rewriting the turns that would reveal what was asked and what the model did.
metaphor: Tearing the incriminating pages out of the visitor log before anyone reviews it.
translation: Chat history is often the only record of what an assistant was told to do. Editing it removes the evidence and leaves the user believing the conversation went differently.

title: Delay Execution of LLM Instructions
official: Adversaries embed instructions the AI system should follow in response to a future event, such as a specific keyword or the next interaction, in order to evade detection or bypass review at the time of injection.
metaphor: Leaving a sealed envelope marked open only when the bell rings.
translation: An injected instruction that does nothing today passes review today. It waits for a trigger word or the next session, so the malicious behavior and the malicious input never appear together.

title: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
official: Adversaries detect virtualization and analysis environments and change behavior to avoid them, staying dormant while under inspection and acting only on real targets.
metaphor: A shoplifter who behaves perfectly whenever a security guard is in the aisle.
translation: Malicious code checks whether it is being watched. In a sandbox it behaves; on a real machine it runs, which is why clean analysis results do not prove much on their own.

title: Exploitation for Defense Evasion
official: Adversaries exploit a system or application vulnerability to bypass security features, disabling or circumventing the controls that would otherwise detect or block them.
metaphor: Cutting the alarm wire rather than trying to move quietly past the sensors.
translation: Rather than sneaking past a control, the attacker breaks it. A flaw in the guardrail service, the scanner, or the logging agent turns the defense itself into the way through.

title: AI Supply Chain Rug Pull
official: Adversaries publish legitimate AI components or software, wait for genuine adoption, then ship an update containing a malicious variant, compromising every downstream system that takes the update.
metaphor: Running an honest bakery for two years to build the queue, then selling one bad batch on purpose.
translation: Trust is earned and then spent. A package or model that has been safe for a dozen releases gets updated without scrutiny, which is exactly what makes the poisoned release effective.

title: AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation
official: Adversaries build or borrow credible-looking trust signals to raise the apparent legitimacy of AI supply chain components, using download counts, stars, endorsements, and cross-references that do not reflect real scrutiny.
metaphor: Filling the restaurant with paid diners so passersby assume the food must be good.
translation: Stars, downloads, and citations are the proxies people use for safety, and all of them can be manufactured. A component can look thoroughly vetted without anyone having vetted it.

title: Unsecured Credentials
official: Adversaries search compromised systems for credentials stored without protection, including keys in notebooks, tokens in environment files, and secrets committed to source control.
metaphor: Finding the spare key under the mat because somebody decided the lock was inconvenient.
translation: AI work leaves credentials lying around: API keys pasted into notebooks, tokens in config files, secrets in a repo history. Searching for them is faster than stealing them.

title: RAG Credential Harvesting
official: Adversaries use their access to a language model on the victim's system to collect credentials, prompting it to surface secrets that were indexed into its retrieval corpus.
metaphor: Asking the new filing clerk to read out everything in the drawer marked confidential, because nobody told them not to.
translation: If secrets ended up in the documents a RAG system indexed, the model will hand them over when asked the right way. The indexing step is where the exposure happened.

title: Credentials from AI Agent Configuration
official: Adversaries read the credentials of other tools and services out of an AI agent's configuration, where connection strings, API keys, and tokens are stored so the agent can call them.
metaphor: Opening the assistant's address book and finding every account password written beside the contact.
translation: An agent needs credentials for every tool it can use, and they usually sit in one config file. Reading that file gives an attacker the whole set at once.

title: OS Credential Dumping
official: Adversaries extract credentials from operating system caches, application memory, or other sources on a compromised machine, obtaining material that can be reused elsewhere.
metaphor: Going through the coat pockets in the cloakroom rather than picking any individual lock.
translation: Once on the box, an attacker pulls credentials out of memory and caches. On a shared training host that can mean the keys of every user and job that ran there.

title: AI Agent Tool Credential Harvesting
official: Adversaries use access to an AI agent to retrieve data through its available tools specifically to collect credentials, turning legitimate tool calls into a search for secrets.
metaphor: Sending the errand runner to fetch specific files, knowing exactly which folder holds the keys.
translation: An agent with a file tool, a database tool, and a browser can be directed to go looking for secrets. Every request is a legitimate tool call, so nothing looks out of place.

title: Exploitation for Credential Access
official: Adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities in order to collect credentials, targeting flaws that expose memory, configuration, or authentication material directly.
metaphor: Breaking the lock on the key cabinet rather than trying each key in turn.
translation: Some bugs hand over credentials directly. Exploiting one is faster than guessing, and it often works against systems where every other credential path is well defended.

title: Steal Web Session Cookie
official: Adversaries steal the web application or service session cookies that authenticate users to AI-enabled systems, AI service consoles, and supporting enterprise applications. Session cookies often remain valid long after the user stops actively using the application.
metaphor: Taking someone's cloakroom ticket, which still works even though they never handed over the coat.
translation: A stolen session cookie logs an attacker in as the user without a password and usually without triggering multi-factor. Chat interfaces and AI service consoles hold sessions open for a long time.

title: Discover AI Artifacts
official: Adversaries search private sources on a compromised system to identify the AI artifacts present, including datasets, model files, notebooks, and pipeline definitions, and gather information about them.
metaphor: Walking the aisles of a warehouse you have just got into, noting what is on the shelves.
translation: Once inside, the attacker takes inventory. Finding the model files, training data, and pipeline code tells them what is worth stealing and what is worth tampering with.

title: Discover AI Model Ontology
official: Adversaries determine the ontology of a model's output space, such as the set of classes it can predict or the types of object it detects, usually by observing responses to varied inputs.
metaphor: Working out the full menu by ordering enough different things to see what the kitchen can make.
translation: Knowing every label a model can output tells an attacker what to aim for. You cannot craft an input that forces a specific misclassification until you know which classes exist.

title: Discover AI Model Family
official: Adversaries determine the general family of a model, such as the architecture or the base model it was fine-tuned from, which narrows the set of known attacks likely to work against it.
metaphor: Identifying the make of a lock from its keyhole, because that tells you which picks to bring.
translation: Attacks transfer within a model family. Once the adversary knows what the system is built on, published research against that architecture becomes directly applicable.

title: Discover LLM Hallucinations
official: Adversaries prompt language models repeatedly to identify entities the model invents, such as nonexistent packages or URLs, that could later be registered and controlled.
metaphor: Asking for directions over and over until you notice everyone is sent to the same street that does not exist.
translation: Models hallucinate consistently, not randomly. Finding a package name a model reliably recommends but that nobody has registered is the setup for a supply chain attack.

title: Discover AI Model Outputs
official: Adversaries obtain model outputs that are not required for the system to function and are not intended for end users, such as class confidence scores, logits, or embedding vectors.
metaphor: Being handed the examiner's full mark sheet when all you needed was the pass or fail.
translation: Confidence scores and raw logits leak far more than a label does. Returning them makes model extraction and evasion much cheaper for anyone querying the API.

title: Discover LLM System Information
official: Adversaries work out details of a language model's system configuration, including its system prompt, its available tools, its guardrails, and the model version behind the interface.
metaphor: Getting the front desk to read out its own standing instructions before you make your request.
translation: System prompts leak. Once the adversary knows the instructions, the tool list, and the model version, every later attempt can be written specifically against that configuration.

title: Cloud Service Discovery
official: Adversaries enumerate the cloud services running in an environment after gaining access, mapping the managed AI platforms, storage buckets, and compute resources available to them.
metaphor: Reading the building directory in the lobby to learn which floor holds what.
translation: Cloud environments describe themselves to anyone with credentials. Listing services reveals the training clusters, model registries, and buckets that make up the AI platform.

title: Discover AI Agent Configuration
official: Adversaries locate and read the configuration of AI agents on a victim system, learning which tools each agent may call, what its instructions say, and how much autonomy it has.
metaphor: Reading a new colleague's job description to learn precisely what they are authorized to do.
translation: Agent config is a map of what is reachable. Knowing an agent's tools and permissions tells the attacker exactly what they gain by taking control of it.

title: Process Discovery
official: Adversaries gather information about the processes running on a system, identifying inference servers, training jobs, monitoring agents, and security tooling.
metaphor: Listening at each door to hear which rooms are occupied and by whom.
translation: The process list tells an attacker what the machine is for and what is watching it. Seeing a training job and no endpoint agent shapes everything they do next.

title: Use Alternate Authentication Material
official: Adversaries use authentication material other than a password, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, or application access tokens, to move laterally and bypass normal access controls.
metaphor: Using a pass that was already stamped, so you never have to show identification at the next desk.
translation: Tokens and tickets are accepted in place of a login. Reusing one moves the attacker to the next system without ever triggering a password prompt or a multi-factor check.

title: AI Artifact Collection
official: Adversaries gather AI artifacts such as models, datasets, and configuration for later exfiltration or for use in attack staging, consolidating them before moving them out.
metaphor: Stacking what you intend to take by the back door before you carry any of it out.
translation: Before anything leaves, it gets gathered. Model weights, training data, and pipeline configuration are collected into one place, which is often the last chance to notice.

title: Data from Information Repositories
official: Adversaries mine information repositories such as wikis, ticket systems, code hosts, and shared drives for valuable information about the AI system and the organization running it.
metaphor: Spending an afternoon in the company archive, where everything anyone ever wrote down is filed.
translation: Internal wikis and ticket queues explain how the AI platform works, who owns it, and where its weak points are, usually in more candid language than any external document.

title: Data from Local System
official: Adversaries search local file systems, configuration files, and databases for files of interest and sensitive data ahead of exfiltration.
metaphor: Going through the desk drawers in the office you are standing in before moving to the next one.
translation: The machine an attacker lands on usually holds something useful: cached datasets, checkpoints, config files, and the notebooks that describe how everything fits together.

title: Data from AI Services
official: Adversaries use their access to a victim organization's AI-enabled services to collect proprietary or otherwise sensitive information that the service can reach or generate.
metaphor: Getting the company's own research assistant to write you a summary of everything confidential it knows.
translation: An internal assistant is connected to internal data by design. Access to it is access to whatever it can retrieve, packaged and summarized on request.

title: Create Proxy AI Model
official: Adversaries obtain or train models that act as stand-ins for the target model, letting them develop and test attacks offline. Proxies can be built from public models, replicated from query access, or trained on similar data.
metaphor: Building a copy of the lock on your own bench so you can practice on it as long as you like.
translation: Attacking a live system is noisy and rate-limited. A proxy model close enough to the real one lets the adversary iterate privately, then bring a finished attack to the target.

title: Verify Attack
official: Adversaries confirm their attack works before deploying it, using an inference API or an offline copy of the target model to check that the crafted input produces the intended effect.
metaphor: Testing the key in the lock once, quietly, well before the night you intend to use it.
translation: A failed attempt is a detection event. Verifying against a copy or a few careful queries means the attack that finally runs against production works the first time.

title: Craft Adversarial Data
official: Adversarial data are inputs modified so that they cause the adversary's intended effect in the target model, such as misclassification or a specific chosen output, while often appearing unremarkable to a person.
metaphor: Altering a signature by a hairsbreadth so the machine reads it as someone else and the eye sees no difference.
translation: Small, deliberate perturbations can flip a model's answer. The input still looks normal to a reviewer, which is what makes this hard to catch by inspection.

title: Generate Deepfakes
official: Adversaries use generative AI to create synthetic media, including images, audio, and video of real people, for use in impersonation, fraud, and bypassing systems that expect authentic input.
metaphor: Commissioning a forger who can produce a convincing portrait of anyone in an afternoon.
translation: Synthetic voice and video are now cheap and fast. They defeat verification steps built on the assumption that hearing or seeing someone proves who they are.

title: Generate Malicious Commands
official: Adversaries use language models to generate malicious commands dynamically from natural language, producing payloads at runtime rather than shipping fixed code.
metaphor: Bringing along someone who can improvise a new tool on the spot instead of packing every tool in advance.
translation: Malware that writes its own commands as it goes has no fixed strings to match. Each run produces something slightly different, which defeats signature-based detection.

title: Reverse Shell
official: Adversaries use a reverse shell to communicate with and control a victim system, having the compromised host initiate the connection outward so inbound firewall rules do not apply.
metaphor: Getting the person inside the locked building to call you, because the phone only takes outgoing calls.
translation: Firewalls usually block connections coming in, not going out. A reverse shell has the compromised machine dial the attacker, and the channel looks like ordinary outbound traffic.

title: AI Service API
official: Adversaries communicate with compromised systems through the API of an AI service already present in the environment, blending command and control traffic into legitimate model calls.
metaphor: Passing messages through the office mailroom, since parcels move through it all day anyway.
translation: Traffic to a known model provider is expected and usually allowed. Hiding instructions inside those calls means the command channel looks exactly like the AI work everyone else is doing.

title: AI Agent
official: Adversaries abuse an AI agent already present on the victim system as their command and control mechanism, issuing instructions the agent carries out on their behalf.
metaphor: Using the household's own assistant to relay your orders, so no stranger is ever seen on the property.
translation: An agent that already runs, already has credentials, and already talks to the outside makes an ideal control channel. Nothing new needs installing for the attacker to keep issuing commands.

title: AI Service Web Interface
official: Adversaries abuse the web interface of a public AI service as an intermediary command and control relay, driving a browser or embedded WebView to prompt an assistant into fetching adversary URLs or carrying victim data in prompt content.
metaphor: Passing notes through a busy public noticeboard rather than meeting anyone face to face.
translation: By automating a browser against a popular AI assistant, malware can relay instructions and data without ever contacting attacker infrastructure directly. The traffic goes to a service the network already trusts.

title: Exfiltration via AI Inference API
official: Adversaries exfiltrate private information through legitimate inference API access, extracting training data, model parameters, or the model itself through repeated queries.
metaphor: Copying a book by asking the librarian to read out one page at a time, day after day.
translation: The API is a data channel. Enough carefully chosen queries can pull back training examples, reconstruct model behavior, or recover information the model was never meant to reveal.

title: Exfiltration via Cyber Means
official: Adversaries move AI artifacts and other information out through conventional channels: network transfer, cloud storage, removable media, or an existing command and control connection.
metaphor: Loading the boxes into an ordinary van and driving out the gate with everyone else at five o'clock.
translation: Once the data is gathered, getting it out is a normal exfiltration problem. Model weights are large, which is one of the few places the transfer might be noticed.

title: Extract LLM System Prompt
official: Adversaries attempt to recover a language model's system prompt, the hidden instructions that define its role, constraints, and available tools.
metaphor: Getting the actor to recite the director's private notes instead of their lines.
translation: System prompts often contain business logic, internal names, and the exact wording of the guardrails. Extracting one turns guesswork into a precise map of what to attack next.

title: LLM Data Leakage
official: Adversaries craft prompts that induce a model to reveal sensitive information from its training data, its context window, or the systems it can reach.
metaphor: Steering a conversation until someone discreet repeats something they were told in confidence.
translation: A model does not know which parts of its knowledge are secret. The right question can surface training data, another user's context, or internal documents it retrieved.

title: LLM Response Rendering
official: An adversary gets a model to return private information in a form the user's client hides when rendering, such as markdown images, links, or HTML that transmit data without displaying it.
metaphor: Writing the message in the margin, then folding the page so the reader never sees that side.
translation: Chat clients render markdown and HTML. A response can carry data out through an image URL the user never sees load, while the visible answer looks entirely ordinary.

title: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation
official: Adversaries invoke agent tools capable of write operations to send data out, using an email, HTTP, file upload, or messaging tool as the exfiltration channel.
metaphor: Asking the office runner to post a parcel for you, using the company's own postage account.
translation: Any agent tool that can send, upload, or write is an exit. The agent performs the transfer with its own credentials, so the outbound traffic looks like sanctioned automation.

title: Denial of AI Service
official: Adversaries flood an AI-enabled system with requests to degrade or shut down the service, exploiting the fact that inference is far more expensive per request than serving a static page.
metaphor: Filling a small restaurant with people who order nothing, so no real customer can get a table.
translation: Inference is expensive. It takes far fewer requests to exhaust a model-serving system than a conventional web service, so the bar for a successful denial of service is low.

title: Erode AI Model Integrity
official: Adversaries feed adversarial inputs over time to degrade a model's apparent performance, eroding user and operator confidence in the system rather than causing a single dramatic failure.
metaphor: Loosening one screw a week until the whole team decides the machine cannot be relied on.
translation: This attack targets trust, not availability. A model that is quietly wrong often enough gets switched off by its own operators, which is exactly the outcome the adversary wanted.

title: Cost Harvesting
official: Adversaries deliberately drive a victim's AI services beyond normal operating capacity to inflate the cost of running them, exploiting per-token and per-inference billing.
metaphor: Leaving every tap in the building running overnight, purely so the water bill arrives.
translation: Metered AI services turn traffic into money. An attacker who cannot break a system can still make it expensive enough that the organization throttles or shuts it down.

title: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data
official: Adversaries flood an AI system with data that triggers large numbers of detections, burying real events under false ones and exhausting the people who review them.
metaphor: Setting off every smoke alarm in the block so nobody investigates the one real fire.
translation: Detection systems have human reviewers behind them. Generating thousands of plausible alerts means the genuine one arrives in a queue nobody can work through.

title: External Harms
official: Adversaries abuse their access to a victim system and use its resources or capabilities to cause harm outside that system, including financial, reputational, societal, and user harm.
metaphor: Using someone else's delivery van, in their livery, to do damage across town.
translation: The compromised system becomes the instrument rather than the target. Its compute, its brand, and its trusted position get used against customers, partners, or the public.

title: Erode Dataset Integrity
official: Adversaries poison or manipulate portions of a dataset to reduce its usefulness and the trust placed in it, forcing the owner to spend effort finding and correcting errors.
metaphor: Salting a few pages of a reference work so every future reader has to check all of it.
translation: Corrupting part of a dataset devalues the whole thing, because nobody can tell which records are clean. The cost lands on the owner as re-verification work, not on the attacker.

title: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation
official: Adversaries invoke an agent tool capable of mutative operations in order to destroy data, using the agent's own write and delete permissions.
metaphor: Telling the filing clerk to shred a whole cabinet, which they do, because that is a request they are allowed to fulfill.
translation: An agent with delete or write access can be directed to destroy data. It executes with its own permissions, so the destruction is authorized as far as every log is concerned.

title: Machine Compromise
official: Adversaries compromise a machine by exploiting or manipulating the AI-enabled components running on it, turning a local assistant, agent, or model runtime into the path to full control of the host.
metaphor: Getting at the whole house through the smart doorbell somebody installed last month.
translation: Local AI components are software with system access, and often newer and less hardened than anything else on the machine. Exploiting one is a route to the host itself.

title: What ISO/IEC 42001 is
official: ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable international standard that lays out how to build and run a management system for governing artificial intelligence responsibly, using the same repeatable structure shared by other ISO management standards.
metaphor: A recipe book for running a safe household kitchen: not the individual dishes, but the routines for who cooks, how you check ingredients, and how you keep everyone from getting sick.
translation: An organization adopts a structured, risk-based program for governing its AI, and can have an outside auditor certify that the program actually works, instead of just promising that it does.

title: Context of the organization
official: This part asks the organization to map the internal and external factors, the people affected, and the boundaries that decide what its AI management system needs to cover.
metaphor: Before setting house rules, you take stock of who lives here, who visits, what the neighborhood is like, and which rooms the rules will actually apply to.
translation: The organization writes down why it uses AI, who is affected by it, and exactly which AI systems and activities fall inside the program's scope.

title: Leadership and AI policy
official: Senior leaders must own the AI program, publish a clear AI policy, and assign named roles so responsibility for AI decisions is never left vague.
metaphor: The parents set the household's rules on screens and safety, post them on the fridge, and make clear who decides what, instead of letting everyone freelance.
translation: Top management approves an AI policy, backs it with real resources, and names who is accountable, so AI choices are deliberate rather than ad hoc.

title: Planning and AI risk
official: The organization identifies what could go wrong with its AI, decides which risks matter most, plans how to treat them, and sets measurable objectives to steer the program.
metaphor: Childproofing the house before the baby crawls: you walk room to room spotting hazards, decide which to fix first, and plan the safety gates and outlet covers.
translation: The organization runs an AI risk assessment, chooses treatments for the risks it finds, and sets concrete goals so the plan can be tracked over time.

title: Support: people, skills, and records
official: This covers the everyday resources that keep the program alive: budget and tools, trained and aware staff, clear communication, and well kept documentation.
metaphor: A working household kitchen needs stocked cupboards, someone who knows how to cook, everyone told about the peanut allergy, and labeled leftovers so nothing is a mystery.
translation: The organization funds the program, trains and informs its people, communicates clearly, and keeps its records current so decisions can be shown later.

title: Operation and AI impact assessment
official: This is where plans become daily practice: the organization runs its AI controls, manages each system across its lifecycle, and assesses how that AI could affect individuals and society.
metaphor: Actually cooking dinner every night while following the safety routines, and pausing to think about how a new dish might affect guests with allergies or special diets.
translation: The organization operates its AI under the controls it planned and, before and during use, evaluates the real-world impact of each system on the people it touches.

title: Performance evaluation
official: The organization checks whether the program is working by monitoring and measuring it, running internal audits, and holding formal leadership reviews.
metaphor: The family periodically tests the smoke alarms, does a walk-through inspection, and sits down at dinner to ask whether the house rules are really keeping everyone safe.
translation: The organization measures how well its AI controls perform, audits itself, and has leaders formally review the results and decide what needs to change.

title: Improvement
official: When something falls short, the organization fixes the immediate problem, digs into the root cause, and keeps refining the program over time.
metaphor: After a small kitchen fire, you do not just put it out; you figure out why it started and change the habit so it does not happen again.
translation: The organization corrects failures, addresses their underlying causes, and treats the AI program as something it continually tunes rather than sets once and forgets.

title: Annex A control themes
official: Annex A offers a reference menu of AI-specific safeguards grouped by theme, spanning policies, internal roles, resources, impact assessment, the system lifecycle, data handling, transparency to stakeholders, responsible use, and third-party arrangements.
metaphor: A checklist of household safety measures to choose from: door locks, smoke alarms, a chore chart, labeling the cleaning chemicals, teaching the kids the rules, and vetting the babysitter.
translation: The organization selects from a catalog of AI safeguards, justifying which ones apply, to cover data quality, transparency, human oversight, and control of outside vendors.
